timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Thank you very much and I should really stay in France longer,
but because already in one day my French has improved tremendously.
I can understand younger people as well as older people.
I was explaining that when I first came that I said yes today,
I've had difficulty understanding younger people
because it tend to mumble.
But older people I could understand,
but now I can understand both the old and the young.
So I feel I have improved a great deal in 24 hours.
I said that it's not true that my father used to put flowers in my hair
because I was two years when my father died and at that time I had no hair.
I was always kept with the, we in Burma we believe that if you shave children's hair,
it grows thick and long.
So at that time I hardly any hair.
My hair was all this shit, if that's why I say it was just a myth allegion.
But I am very touched that people think that he put flowers in my hair.
The reason why I wear flowers in my hair is actually because my mother used to do so.
Because the Burmese used to do so.
This is very much a Burmese tradition that ladies wear women wear flowers
and they're hair, girls wear flowers in their hair.
But these days Burmese girls had started cutting their hair short.
And so they don't longer wear flowers in their hair.
And on top of it, they don't know how to put flowers in their hair
and have great difficulty because my personal assistant has short hair
and doesn't know how to help me.
But I'm very happy to be here and when the minister said that Paris France
signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948,
I'd like to remind everybody that so did Burma,
Burma signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in December 1948
and was one of the first countries in the world to do so.
So we should be committed to upholding all the basic human rights.
And in the beginning, when we first became independent,
we were a democracy, a parliamentary democracy,
and we certainly put a lot of importance on the support for human rights.
These rights were eroded during the years of military rule,
but we hope that we will be able to restore them to their former glory.
And in our struggle to do this, we have been helped greatly by countries like France,
which believe in the basic values that are linked to an acceptance of every human being
to preserve his or her dignity.
I was asked a couple of days ago in London what I thought of people who say
that some countries are not yet fit for democracy.
And I said that in my opinion, if there is just one person in that country
who truly believes in basic human dignity,
then that country is fit for democracy.
But in order to make ourselves familiar with the institutions
as well as the practices of democracy, we need the help of mature democracies.
And this help we have been having in generous measure,
I have been very touched by the warmth,
by the enthusiasm with which people all in all the countries I have visited
since last month have shown with regard to our cause in Thailand,
which is a close neighbor and a fellow member of ASEAN.
I found that the people of Thailand were very much aware of the struggle of the people of Burma.
And although as neighbors, we have little problems,
such as you have with English and the Germans, etc.
I am confident that these problems have been overcome,
and we will be able to work together to make our region part of the world
that respects human rights, not just by word of mouth, but respects it in action.
We have to show that we respect human rights by everyday action in our countries.
And the minister has talked about the recent changes in Burma,
and they have been changes, but these changes need to be maintained.
We are just at the beginning of a road,
and I have emphasized the fact that this is not a road which is ready and waiting for us,
but a road that we will have to build as we go along.
This road is open, but actually like a lot of roads in Burma in very bad condition.
So we must repair and maintain this road as we go along.
And in this work of maintenance and repair,
we will need the help of our friends.
I have repeatedly emphasized the need for development and humanitarian aid and investment,
which are democracy-friendly and human rights-friendly.
That is to say, which are based on such principles as accountability and transparency,
and which keep up and awareness of the reforms that are still needed in our country.
So investment aid, whether development or humanitarian,
should be carefully tailored and calibrated in order to help the process of reform.
I do not think that I need to remind the people of France and the French government
how important our such values as liberty, equality, and fraternity.
But for us, these are still prizes to be won through hard work and through perseverance.
But I have no doubt that with the goodwill of and practical help of friends from all over the world,
we will be able to claim these prizes for our own.
And we need to be extra careful within the next three years,
because 2015 is when the next general elections are.
And before this next general elections, we would like to make sure that Burma is a country
where elections are truly democratic and truly free and fair,
and that that will be a year when the people can say,
we are in a position to shape the destiny of our country.
Thank you.

youtube_channel: French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs
youtube_description:
A l'invitation du Président de la République, Aung San Suu Kyi, Prix Nobel de la Paix, députée au parlement birman et Présidente de la Ligue nationale pour la Démocratie, a effectué une visite en France du 26 au 29 juin 2012.
A l'occasion de cette visite, dernière étape de son premier déplacement en Europe depuis près de 25 ans, la France rend hommage au combat mené par cette femme exceptionnelle en faveur des droits de l'Homme, et marque son appui actif au processus de transition démocratique en cours en Birmanie.
